In June 2000, while visiting Korea, I did a fun hack that clearly illustrates the original and true meaning of the word "hacker".

I went to lunch with some GNU fans, and was sitting down to eat some tteokbokki (*), when a waitress set down six chopsticks right in front of me. It occurred to me that perhaps these were meant for three people, but it was more amusing to imagine that I was supposed to use all six. I did not know any way to do that, so I realized that if I could come up with a way, it would be a hack. I started thinking. After a few seconds I had an idea.

First I used my left hand to put three chopsticks into my right hand. That was not so hard, though I had to figure out where to put them so that I could control them individually. Then I used my right hand to put the other three chopsticks into my left hand. That was hard, since I had to keep the three chopsticks already in my right hand from falling out. After a couple of tries I got it done.

Then I had to figure out how to use the six chopsticks. That was harder. I did not manage well with the left hand, but I succeeded in manipulating all three in the right hand. After a couple of minutes of practice and adjustment, I managed to pick up a piece of food using three sticks converging on it from three different directions, and put it in my mouth.

It didn't become easy—for practical purposes, using two chopsticks is completely superior. But precisely because using three in one hand is hard and ordinarily never thought of, it has "hack value", as my lunch companions immediately recognized. Playfully doing something difficult, whether useful or not, that is hacking.

I later told the Korea story to a friend in Boston, who proceded to put four chopsticks in one hand and use them as two pairs—picking up two different pieces of food at once, one with each pair. He had topped my hack. Was his action, too, a hack? I think so. Is he therefore a hacker? That depends on how much he likes to hack.

The hacking community developed at MIT and some other universities in the 1960s and 1970s. Hacking included a wide range of activities, from writing software, to practical jokes, to exploring the roofs and tunnels of the MIT campus. Other activities, performed far from MIT and far from computers, also fit hackers' idea of what hacking means: for instance, I think the controversial 1950s "musical piece" by John Cage, 4'33" (****), is more of a hack than a musical composition. The palindromic three-part piece written by Guillaume de Machaut in the 1300s, "Ma Fin Est Mon Commencement", was also a good hack, even better because it also sounds good as music. Puck appreciated hack value.

It is hard to write a simple definition of something as varied as hacking, but I think what these activities have in common is playfulness, cleverness, and exploration. Thus, hacking means exploring the limits of what is possible, in a spirit of playful cleverness. Activities that display playful cleverness have "hack value".

The concept of hacking excludes wit and art as such. The people who began to speak of their activities as "hacking" were familiar with wit and art, and with the names of the various fields of those; they were also doing something else, something different, for which they came up with the name "hacking". Thus, composing a funny joke or a beautiful piece of music may well involve playful cleverness, but a joke as such and a piece of music as such are not hacks, however funny or beautiful they may be. However, if the piece is a palindrome, we can say it is a hack as well as music; if the piece is vacuous, we can say it is a hack on music.

Hackers typically had little respect for the silly rules that administrators like to impose, so they looked for ways around. For instance, when computers at MIT started to have "security" (that is, restrictions on what users could do), some hackers found clever ways to bypass the security, partly so they could use the computers freely, and partly just for the sake of cleverness (hacking does not need to be useful). However, only some hackers did this—many were occupied with other kinds of cleverness, such as placing some amusing object on top of MIT's great dome (**), finding a way to do a certain computation with only 5 instructions when the shortest known program required 6, writing a program to print numbers in roman numerals, or writing a program to understand questions in English. (Hacking does not have to be without practical use.)

Meanwhile, another group of hackers at MIT found a different solution to the problem of computer security: they designed the Incompatible Timesharing System without security "features". In the hacker's paradise, the glory days of the Artificial Intelligence Lab, there was no security breaking, because there was no security to break. It was there, in that environment, that I learned to be a hacker, though I had shown the inclination previously. We had plenty of other domains in which to be playfully clever, without building artificial security obstacles which then had to be overcome.

Yet when I say I am a hacker, people often think I am making a naughty admission, presenting myself specifically as a security breaker. How did this confusion develop?

Around 1980, when the news media took notice of hackers, they fixated on one narrow aspect of real hacking: the security breaking which some hackers occasionally did. They ignored all the rest of hacking, and took the term to mean breaking security, no more and no less. The media have since spread that definition, disregarding our attempts to correct them. As a result, most people have a mistaken idea of what we hackers actually do and what we think.

You can help correct the misunderstanding simply by making a distinction between security breaking and hacking—by using the term "cracking" for security breaking. The people who do it are "crackers" (***). Some of them may also be hackers, just as some of them may be chess players or golfers; most of them are not.

Happy hacking.

* Pronounced like stuckbokekey minus the s (with an unaspirated t), if I recall right.

** Going on the great dome is "forbidden", so in a sense it constitutes "breaking security". Nonetheless, the MIT Museum proudly presents photos of some of the best dome hacks, as well as some of the objects that hackers placed on the dome in their hacks. The MIT administration thus implicitly recognizes that "breaking security" is not inherently evil and need not be invariably condemned. Whether security breaking is wrong depends on what the security breaker proceeds to do with the "forbidden" access thus obtained. Hurting people is bad, amusing the community is good.

*** I coined the term "cracker" in the early 80s when I saw journalists were equating "hacker" with "security breaker".

The campaign to reclaim the word "hacker" from association with security breaking is doing pretty well, as witness the widespread usage of terms such as "hacklab" and "hackathon".

**** The piece 4'33" is trivial in the mathematical sense. For each "movement", the pianist opens the keyboard cover, waits the appropriate amount of time, then closes it; that's all. It is a musical counterpart of the empty set.

Here are some examples of fun hacks. If they make you smile, you're a hacker at heart.

First, some of mine.

  • I learned to use two pairs of chopsticks in one hand, imitating my friend. Here I demonstrate this.

  • Speaking of chopsticks, some kinds of Italian grissini work fine as chopsticks — then, after the meal, you can eat them. I brought a bag of them to Taiwan once just to show them that Italy has chopsticks too.

  • Customer Training College changed to Customer Draining College. Sassy, not computer-related.

  • In 1981, Newsweek interviewed me for an article on hackers. When their photographer arrived, I decided the article should contain a real hack, so I put on the folk dance performing group's Bulgarian dance costume and held hands with a tentacle-like disused robot arm to give the impression I was dancing in a line with a robot. Sadly, they cropped the photo so that little of the robot arm is visible, and it may not be obvious what we are doing together.

  • Photos of some other hacks I've done are here.

    An anonymous friend joined me to place the "Barbidall Square" sign on a lamppost at Wellesley College, near the stop for the bus to Kendall Square near MIT. With one single sign we made fun of Wellesley students and of MIT students, in different ways! The sign was removed after a few days, presumably by vandalls.

  • In India there is a chain of fine Bengali restaurants called "Oh! Calcutta". The staff, and the clients, have no idea why that expression is notorious. During my 2014 visit to India I decided to educate them by bringing to the restaurant printouts of the painting itself and a publicity photo from the play. I left a copy of each with the staff.

  • Many years ago I had a root canal operation in a molar in the back of my mouth. It was difficult for me to keep my mouth open far enough, and the dentist said this was because I had a rather small mouth.

    When it was done, I had him sign a testimonial affirming this fact. I gave it to my mother to show she was wrong about me, all those years when she said I had a big mouth.

  • My puns and verse and song parodies are also playful cleverness, but the word "hack" does not include verbal wit.

  • April fools such as Yellow Hat GNU/Linux and Pre-Zen studies are on the border between hacking and wit, because they involve an element of action (fooling someone), not just presenting amusing words.

Other people's hacks.

  • Reporters make a game of inventing amusing prases to avoid using an unusual noun twice in the same article.
  • Protesters against driverless taxis immobilize them by putting cones on them.

    The article says that "there's no evidence that the companies are working in tandem with law enforcement to record everyone all the time." That may be true, but the cases do record the people around them. If they do not systematically send the images to repression orgamizations now, that could always be set up in the future.

  • Two researchers asked GPT-3 to write a paper about GPT-3, then submitted it for publication listing GPT-3 as the first author.
  • Everyone's first hack: walking in the wrong direction on an escalator. That's not the way it's designed to be used, but can you make it work?
  • Fighting racism with the hacker spirit: a coloring book entitled "Some of my best friends are colored."

  • Saving Jews from Nazi death camps by diagnosing them with highly contagious "Syndrome K".

    Protecting people from genocide is as serious as a project can be, but there's room for playful cleverness in bending the rules to achieve it.

  • I think this award-winning art project was actually a hack.
  • Medicine hackers distribute instructions for manufacturing medicines to avoid the intolerable prices of the US pharma industry.
  • A robot that climbs windows to deploy a sun shade. Pure, sweet, and computer-based.
  • Getting potholes repaired by painting penises around them.
  • Making potholes in the streets of Panama City send tweets asking to be repaired.
  • Hoisting Nigerian scammers on their own petard. Cunning, mischievous, and not using computers except for email and phone calls.
  • Using chatbots to fool and waste the time of scam callers. In this special situation, a program that pretends to be human in order to deceive people is morally legitimate, because it obstructs their attempts to commit a real wrong.
  • Lady Gaga's approach to clothing seems like hacking to me.
  • The band Van Halen put a requirement in its gig contracts to supply M&Ms with the brown ones removed. This was a clever way of determining at a glance whether the people running the venue had really tried to carry out the other requirements, which were necessary to avoid expensive damage to facilities.

    You could call it a "laziness canary".

  • Threatin: Band Creates Fake Fanbase for Tour Attended by No One.

    This was quite bizarre, but seems to have caused some real problems for the music venues that were misled.

  • The Piet painting programming language is the most bizarre programming language hack I have ever seen. It is totally unusable if your goal is a maintainable program for practical use, but wow what hack value!

  • A charming hack in the London Underground.

  • In challenge-level square dance, the caller invents combinations of meta-calls, and the dancers have to figure out very quickly what those calls mean in terms of physical motion. It is not easy, and the set gets messed up from time to time. One caller at MIT around 1980 had a habit of saying "damn it" when that happened.

    The dancers were more or less the same group at each session, and being at MIT, they decided to hack the caller: they defined "damn it" as a call, but didn't tell him. They defined the call to mean, "Change places with your corner" — chosen because it would never help clean up the mess. Subsequently, each time he said "damn it," he got a puzzling surprise.

  • The hacker who made this poster was arrested for it.

  • Chindogu, "unuseless inventions", are subtly absurd hacks.

  • Dilbert: Japanese workers hack credulous US managers.

  • TicBot is a conversation hack.

  • The ultimate series of hacks with ordinary everyday objects appears in the 1987 film, Der Lauf der Dinge, by Fischli and Weiss. (This should not be confused with the unrelated 2006 film by the same name.)

  • Although hacking and cracking are conceptually unrelated, occasionally they are found together. This is hacking that involves some cracking.

    This hack pointed out the injustice of the laws against "child" pornography, which is good, but doing that by causing other people to be jailed seems wrong to me. (Hacks can raise ethical issues just as other activities do; cleverness and playfulness do not guarantee that one can do no wrong.) It is also foolhardy to taunt a dangerous monster.

  • Hacking a Casio calculator with a hard-to-notice second display screen, and internet connectivity, to make it an ideal device for cheating on exams.

    I don't approve of cheating on real exams, but the hack is impressive. Besides, if you can design something like this, you can ace your exams honestly.

  • A fun hack implemented via cracking: making a TV emergency alert system give warnings about dead bodies emerging from graves.

    The security holes that made this possible might be used humorlessly to do real harm, but this hack didn't harm anyone.

  • You can make Nike's running-map server display whatever drawing you like by running on properly chosen streets.

  • "Rooftoppers" scale tall buildings just for the hack of it. I don't share, and can't understand, their desire for risk, but that doesn't alter the fact that this is hacking.

  • Acción Ortográfica Quito corrects punctuation and grammar in graffiti.

  • A German student filed a freedom of information request to get the questions for an exam he will have to take.

  • A hacker arranged to play music by printing on a dot-matrix printer. Here's one with a line printer. Note that the line printer is not being told to advance the paper.

  • Japanese artist Megumi Igarashi is on trial for distributing 3d-printed models of her genitals.

    She also built a kayak using that shape. Paddling such a kayak would enable certain fetishists to feel they are really inside her.

  • Airline "hobbyists" hack the rules of frequent flier miles to get lots of air travel without ever needing to pay.

    I appreciate the cleverness of these hacks, but repeating the hack every day seems pointless as well as extremely wasteful — like an addiction. Once should be enough.

  • Russian pranksters fooled Elton John by phoning him and pretending to be President Putin.

  • Shoppers at Zara stores found clothes with labels saying, "I Made This... But Didn't Get Paid".
  • Lenny the robo-answerer can waste the time of robo-callers. As of January 2018 you can phone Lenny at +1 347-514-7296.
  • A kea (New Zealand parrot) learned to trigger traps meant to catch stoats. Apparently it did this just as play, because it did not take the bait from the traps.
  • A single fake fingerprint can match 20% of all real fingerprints, in many fingerprint authentication systems.
  • Doordash has a scheme where it discounts pizza for customers but pays the restaurant full price. (This is a scheme to mislead and trap restaurant owners for the long term.)

    One restaurant owner started ordering pizzas from his own restaurant via Doordash, and making money from Doordash on each one.

  • A student housing project in Stuttgart was built by student residents, and the current residents continue to maintain it and change it.
  • An example of using recorded messages to waste telemarketer's time.
  • The Satanic Temple is a hack to oppose creeping establishment of religion.
  • In the short story, "'Repent, Harlequin!' Said the Ticktockman," by Harlan Ellison, the Harlequin's acts of resistance are hacks. I read it around 1970. Although I did not think of the story often after that, I believe it was an inspiration for my idea of hacking, and the idea of using it for resisting injustice.
  • In the movie Brazil, the unauthorized plumbing repairman is a hacker.

  • One hacker started taping bananas to walls and selling them as "art" for over $100,000. Then another hacker stunned the art world by eating one of these pieces of edible "art".

    I have eaten, a few times, in a restaurant in Madrid whose desserts struck me as works of visual art. Not just pretend art, like those bananas, but real art with real beauty. To eat my dessert, I had to overcome my upbringing which taught me that one must not damage an art work.

  • *Musicians Algorithmically Generate Every Possible [short] Melody, Release Them to Public Domain.*

  • Artist protests using fake real estate images — and dupes investors.
  • Fake street signs projected onto buildings fool car AI in 1/10 second; humans can hardly see them.
  • Berlin artist uses 99 phones to trick Google into traffic jam alert.
  • The conman (Trump) was tricked into being photographed with a humorously altered version of the US presidential seal.

  • Dolly Parton once competed in a drag queen Dolly Parton look-alike contest, and came in last.

    I think she appreciated the hack value of this.

  • These real-life Rube Goldberg machines are a delightful hack. It's a shame that Herscher doesn't describe this as hacking, but they teach people to appreciate hack value.

  • Belarus hackers cracked Belarusian railroad computers to interfere with Russian troop trains. They say they can crash the signaling and emergency control systems and may do that later.

    The specific activity they are doing, breaking security on systems, is called "cracking", but I refer to them as "hackers" because they seem to have the hacker spirit.

    They say they are using ransomware, but not demanding money — instead, they demand freeing political prisoners.

  • Birds Aren't Real: a pretend conspiracist movement.

  • The music (and performance art) group Two Shell treats all contact with the public as an opportunity for befuddling hacks.

You can make Nike's running-map server display whatever drawing you like by running on properly chosen streets. "Rooftoppers" scale tall buildings just for the hack of it. I don't share, and can't understand, their desire for risk, but that doesn't alter the fact that this is hacking. Acción Ortográfica Quito corrects punctuation and grammar in graffiti. A German student filed a freedom of information request to get the questions for an exam he will have to take. A hacker arranged to play music by printing on a dot-matrix printer. Here's one with a line printer. Note that the line printer is not being told to advance the paper. Japanese artist Megumi Igarashi is on trial for distributing 3d-printed models of her genitals. She also built a kayak using that shape. Paddling such a kayak would enable certain fetishists to feel they are really inside her. Airline "hobbyists" hack the rules of frequent flier miles to get lots of air travel without ever needing to pay. I appreciate the cleverness of these hacks, but repeating the hack every day seems pointless as well as extremely wasteful — like an addiction. Once should be enough. Russian pranksters fooled Elton John by phoning him and pretending to be President Putin. Shoppers at Zara stores found clothes with labels saying, "I Made This... But Didn't Get Paid". Lenny the robo-answerer can waste the time of robo-callers. As of January 2018 you can phone Lenny at +1 347-514-7296. A kea (New Zealand parrot) learned to trigger traps meant to catch stoats. Apparently it did this just as play, because it did not take the bait from the traps. A single fake fingerprint can match 20% of all real fingerprints, in many fingerprint authentication systems. Doordash has a scheme where it discounts pizza for customers but pays the restaurant full price. (This is a scheme to mislead and trap restaurant owners for the long term.) One restaurant owner started ordering pizzas from his own restaurant via Doordash, and making money from Doordash on each one. A student housing project in Stuttgart was built by student residents, and the current residents continue to maintain it and change it. An example of using recorded messages to waste telemarketer's time. The Satanic Temple is a hack to oppose creeping establishment of religion. In the short story, "'Repent, Harlequin!' Said the Ticktockman," by Harlan Ellison, the Harlequin's acts of resistance are hacks. I read it around 1970. Although I did not think of the story often after that, I believe it was an inspiration for my idea of hacking, and the idea of using it for resisting injustice. In the movie Brazil, the unauthorized plumbing repairman is a hacker. One hacker started taping bananas to walls and selling them as "art" for over $100,000. Then another hacker stunned the art world by eating one of these pieces of edible "art". I have eaten, a few times, in a restaurant in Madrid whose desserts struck me as works of visual art. Not just pretend art, like those bananas, but real art with real beauty. To eat my dessert, I had to overcome my upbringing which taught me that one must not damage an art work. *Musicians Algorithmically Generate Every Possible [short] Melody, Release Them to Public Domain.* Artist protests using fake real estate images — and dupes investors. Fake street signs projected onto buildings fool car AI in 1/10 second; humans can hardly see them. Berlin artist uses 99 phones to trick Google into traffic jam alert. The conman (Trump) was tricked into being photographed with a humorously altered version of the US presidential seal. Dolly Parton once competed in a drag queen Dolly Parton look-alike contest, and came in last. I think she appreciated the hack value of this. These real-life Rube Goldberg machines are a delightful hack. It's a shame that Herscher doesn't describe this as hacking, but they teach people to appreciate hack value. Belarus hackers cracked Belarusian railroad computers to interfere with Russian troop trains. They say they can crash the signaling and emergency control systems and may do that later. The specific activity they are doing, breaking security on systems, is called "cracking", but I refer to them as "hackers" because they seem to have the hacker spirit. They say they are using ransomware, but not demanding money — instead, they demand freeing political prisoners. Birds Aren't Real: a pretend conspiracist movement. The music (and performance art) group Two Shell treats all contact with the public as an opportunity for befuddling hacks. Return to Richard Stallman's home page. blocks.html_en: In June 2000, while visiting Korea, I did a fun hack that clearly illustrates the original and true meaning of the word "hacker".

sentences.en: In June 2000, while visiting Korea, I did a fun hack that clearly illustrates the original and true meaning of the word "hacker".
sentences.zh: 2000年6月，在访问韩国时，我做了一次有趣的黑客活动，清楚地说明了“黑客”一词的原始和真正含义。

blocks.html_en: I went to lunch with some GNU fans, and was sitting down to eat some tteokbokki (*), when a waitress set down six chopsticks right in front of me. It occurred to me that perhaps these were meant for three people, but it was more amusing to imagine that I was supposed to use all six. I did not know any way to do that, so I realized that if I could come up with a way, it would be a hack. I started thinking. After a few seconds I had an idea.

sentences.en: I went to lunch with some GNU fans, and was sitting down to eat some tteokbokki (*), when a waitress set down six chopsticks right in front of me.
sentences.zh: 我和一些 GNU 粉丝一起去吃午饭，正坐下来吃一些炒年糕 (*)，这时一位女服务员在我面前放下了六根筷子。

sentences.en: It occurred to me that perhaps these were meant for three people, but it was more amusing to imagine that I was supposed to use all six.
sentences.zh: 我突然想到，也许这些是为三个人准备的，但更有趣的是想象我应该使用所有六个人。

sentences.en: I did not know any way to do that, so I realized that if I could come up with a way, it would be a hack.
sentences.zh: 我不知道有什么方法可以做到这一点，所以我意识到如果我能想出一种方法，那就是一种破解。

sentences.en: I started thinking.
sentences.zh: 我开始思考。

sentences.en: After a few seconds I had an idea.
sentences.zh: 几秒钟后我有了一个想法。

blocks.html_en: First I used my left hand to put three chopsticks into my right hand. That was not so hard, though I had to figure out where to put them so that I could control them individually. Then I used my right hand to put the other three chopsticks into my left hand. That was hard, since I had to keep the three chopsticks already in my right hand from falling out. After a couple of tries I got it done.

sentences.en: First I used my left hand to put three chopsticks into my right hand.
sentences.zh: 首先我用左手把三根筷子放到右手里。

sentences.en: That was not so hard, though I had to figure out where to put them so that I could control them individually.
sentences.zh: 这并不难，尽管我必须弄清楚将它们放在哪里以便我可以单独控制它们。

sentences.en: Then I used my right hand to put the other three chopsticks into my left hand.
sentences.zh: 然后我用右手把另外三根筷子放到了左手上。

sentences.en: That was hard, since I had to keep the three chopsticks already in my right hand from falling out.
sentences.zh: 这很困难，因为我必须防止右手已有的三根筷子掉下来。

sentences.en: After a couple of tries I got it done.
sentences.zh: 经过几次尝试，我完成了。

blocks.html_en: Then I had to figure out how to use the six chopsticks. That was harder. I did not manage well with the left hand, but I succeeded in manipulating all three in the right hand. After a couple of minutes of practice and adjustment, I managed to pick up a piece of food using three sticks converging on it from three different directions, and put it in my mouth.

sentences.en: Then I had to figure out how to use the six chopsticks.
sentences.zh: 然后我必须弄清楚如何使用这六根筷子。

sentences.en: That was harder.
sentences.zh: 那更难了。

sentences.en: I did not manage well with the left hand, but I succeeded in manipulating all three in the right hand.
sentences.zh: 我的左手控制得不太好，但我右手却成功地操纵了这三个动作。

sentences.en: After a couple of minutes of practice and adjustment, I managed to pick up a piece of food using three sticks converging on it from three different directions, and put it in my mouth.
sentences.zh: 经过几分钟的练习和调整，我成功地用三根棍子从三个不同的方向汇聚在一块食物上，夹起一块食物，放进嘴里。

blocks.html_en: It didn't become easy—for practical purposes, using two chopsticks is completely superior. But precisely because using three in one hand is hard and ordinarily never thought of, it has "hack value", as my lunch companions immediately recognized. Playfully doing something difficult, whether useful or not, that is hacking.

sentences.en: It didn't become easy—for practical purposes, using two chopsticks is completely superior.
sentences.zh: 这并不容易——出于实用目的，使用两根筷子是完全优越的。

sentences.en: But precisely because using three in one hand is hard and ordinarily never thought of, it has "hack value", as my lunch companions immediately recognized.
sentences.zh: 但正是因为一只手使用三个是困难的并且通常从未想到过，所以它具有“黑客价值”，正如我的午餐同伴立即意识到的那样。

sentences.en: Playfully doing something difficult, whether useful or not, that is hacking.
sentences.zh: 开玩笑地做一些困难的事情，无论有用与否，那就是黑客行为。

blocks.html_en: I later told the Korea story to a friend in Boston, who proceded to put four chopsticks in one hand and use them as two pairs—picking up two different pieces of food at once, one with each pair. He had topped my hack. Was his action, too, a hack? I think so. Is he therefore a hacker? That depends on how much he likes to hack.

sentences.en: I later told the Korea story to a friend in Boston, who proceded to put four chopsticks in one hand and use them as two pairs—picking up two different pieces of food at once, one with each pair.
sentences.zh: 后来我向波士顿的一位朋友讲述了韩国的故事，他把四根筷子放在一只手上，并把它们分成两对——同时夹起两块不同的食物，每双一根。

sentences.en: He had topped my hack.
sentences.zh: 他已经超越了我的黑客。

sentences.en: Was his action, too, a hack?
sentences.zh: 他的行为也是黑客行为吗？

sentences.en: I think so.
sentences.zh: 我想是的。

sentences.en: Is he therefore a hacker?
sentences.zh: 那么他是一名黑客吗？

sentences.en: That depends on how much he likes to hack.
sentences.zh: 这取决于他有多喜欢黑客。

blocks.html_en: The hacking community developed at MIT and some other universities in the 1960s and 1970s. Hacking included a wide range of activities, from writing software, to practical jokes, to exploring the roofs and tunnels of the MIT campus. Other activities, performed far from MIT and far from computers, also fit hackers' idea of what hacking means: for instance, I think the controversial 1950s "musical piece" by John Cage, 4'33" (****), is more of a hack than a musical composition. The palindromic three-part piece written by Guillaume de Machaut in the 1300s, "Ma Fin Est Mon Commencement", was also a good hack, even better because it also sounds good as music. Puck appreciated hack value.

sentences.en: The hacking community developed at MIT and some other universities in the 1960s and 1970s.
sentences.zh: 黑客社区在 20 世纪 60 年代和 1970 年代在麻省理工学院和其他一些大学发展起来。

sentences.en: Hacking included a wide range of activities, from writing software, to practical jokes, to exploring the roofs and tunnels of the MIT campus.
sentences.zh: 黑客活动涉及范围广泛，从编写软件到恶作剧，再到探索麻省理工学院校园的屋顶和隧道。

sentences.en: Other activities, performed far from MIT and far from computers, also fit hackers' idea of what hacking means: for instance, I think the controversial 1950s "musical piece" by John Cage, 4'33" (****), is more of a hack than a musical composition.
sentences.zh: 其他远离麻省理工学院、远离计算机进行的活动也符合黑客对黑客行为的理解：例如，我认为约翰·凯奇 (John Cage) 创作的备受争议的 20 世纪 50 年代“音乐作品”，4'33" (****)，与其说是音乐作品，不如说是黑客行为。

sentences.en: The palindromic three-part piece written by Guillaume de Machaut in the 1300s, "Ma Fin Est Mon Commencement", was also a good hack, even better because it also sounds good as music.
sentences.zh: 纪尧姆·德·马肖 (Guillaume de Machaut) 在 1300 年代创作的回文三部分作品“Ma Fin Est Mon Commencement”也是一个很好的技巧，甚至更好，因为它作为音乐听起来也很不错。

sentences.en: Puck appreciated hack value.
sentences.zh: 帕克很欣赏黑客的价值。

blocks.html_en: It is hard to write a simple definition of something as varied as hacking, but I think what these activities have in common is playfulness, cleverness, and exploration. Thus, hacking means exploring the limits of what is possible, in a spirit of playful cleverness. Activities that display playful cleverness have "hack value".

sentences.en: It is hard to write a simple definition of something as varied as hacking, but I think what these activities have in common is playfulness, cleverness, and exploration.
sentences.zh: 很难为黑客这样多种多样的活动写出一个简单的定义，但我认为这些活动的共同点是好玩、聪明和探索。

sentences.en: Thus, hacking means exploring the limits of what is possible, in a spirit of playful cleverness.
sentences.zh: 因此，黑客意味着本着俏皮聪明的精神探索可能性的极限。

sentences.en: Activities that display playful cleverness have "hack value".
sentences.zh: 表现出俏皮聪明的活动具有“黑客价值”。

blocks.html_en: The concept of hacking excludes wit and art as such. The people who began to speak of their activities as "hacking" were familiar with wit and art, and with the names of the various fields of those; they were also doing something else, something different, for which they came up with the name "hacking". Thus, composing a funny joke or a beautiful piece of music may well involve playful cleverness, but a joke as such and a piece of music as such are not hacks, however funny or beautiful they may be. However, if the piece is a palindrome, we can say it is a hack as well as music; if the piece is vacuous, we can say it is a hack on music.

sentences.en: The concept of hacking excludes wit and art as such.
sentences.zh: 黑客的概念排除了智慧和艺术本身。

sentences.en: The people who began to speak of their activities as "hacking" were familiar with wit and art, and with the names of the various fields of those; they were also doing something else, something different, for which they came up with the name "hacking".
sentences.zh: 那些开始将他们的活动称为“黑客”的人们熟悉智慧和艺术，以及这些领域的各个领域的名称；他们还做了一些其他的事情，一些不同的事情，为此他们想出了“黑客”这个名字。

sentences.en: Thus, composing a funny joke or a beautiful piece of music may well involve playful cleverness, but a joke as such and a piece of music as such are not hacks, however funny or beautiful they may be.
sentences.zh: 因此，创作一个有趣的笑话或一首优美的音乐很可能需要俏皮的聪明才智，但一个笑话本身和一首音乐本身并不是黑客，无论它们多么有趣或美丽。

sentences.en: However, if the piece is a palindrome, we can say it is a hack as well as music; if the piece is vacuous, we can say it is a hack on music.
sentences.zh: 然而，如果这首曲子是回文，我们可以说它是黑客，也是音乐；如果这首曲子是空洞的，我们可以说它是对音乐的黑客攻击。

blocks.html_en: Hackers typically had little respect for the silly rules that administrators like to impose, so they looked for ways around. For instance, when computers at MIT started to have "security" (that is, restrictions on what users could do), some hackers found clever ways to bypass the security, partly so they could use the computers freely, and partly just for the sake of cleverness (hacking does not need to be useful). However, only some hackers did this—many were occupied with other kinds of cleverness, such as placing some amusing object on top of MIT's great dome (**), finding a way to do a certain computation with only 5 instructions when the shortest known program required 6, writing a program to print numbers in roman numerals, or writing a program to understand questions in English. (Hacking does not have to be without practical use.)

sentences.en: Hackers typically had little respect for the silly rules that administrators like to impose, so they looked for ways around.
sentences.zh: 黑客通常不太尊重管理员喜欢强加的愚蠢规则，因此他们寻找解决方法。

sentences.en: For instance, when computers at MIT started to have "security" (that is, restrictions on what users could do), some hackers found clever ways to bypass the security, partly so they could use the computers freely, and partly just for the sake of cleverness (hacking does not need to be useful).
sentences.zh: 例如，当麻省理工学院的计算机开始具有“安全性”（即对用户可以做什么的限制）时，一些黑客找到了绕过安全性的巧妙方法，部分是为了他们可以自由地使用计算机，部分只是为了聪明（黑客攻击不一定有用）。

sentences.en: However, only some hackers did this—many were occupied with other kinds of cleverness, such as placing some amusing object on top of MIT's great dome (**), finding a way to do a certain computation with only 5 instructions when the shortest known program required 6, writing a program to print numbers in roman numerals, or writing a program to understand questions in English.

sentences.en: (Hacking does not have to be without practical use.)
sentences.zh: （黑客攻击不一定没有实际用途。）

blocks.html_en: Meanwhile, another group of hackers at MIT found a different solution to the problem of computer security: they designed the Incompatible Timesharing System without security "features". In the hacker's paradise, the glory days of the Artificial Intelligence Lab, there was no security breaking, because there was no security to break. It was there, in that environment, that I learned to be a hacker, though I had shown the inclination previously. We had plenty of other domains in which to be playfully clever, without building artificial security obstacles which then had to be overcome.

sentences.en: Meanwhile, another group of hackers at MIT found a different solution to the problem of computer security: they designed the Incompatible Timesharing System without security "features".
sentences.zh: 与此同时，麻省理工学院的另一组黑客找到了解决计算机安全问题的不同解决方案：他们设计了没有安全“功能”的不兼容分时系统。

sentences.en: In the hacker's paradise, the glory days of the Artificial Intelligence Lab, there was no security breaking, because there was no security to break.
sentences.zh: 在黑客的天堂、人工智能实验室的辉煌岁月里，没有安全漏洞，因为没有安全可破解。

sentences.en: It was there, in that environment, that I learned to be a hacker, though I had shown the inclination previously.
sentences.zh: 正是在那里，在那种环境下，我学会了成为一名黑客，尽管我之前已经表现出了这种倾向。

sentences.en: We had plenty of other domains in which to be playfully clever, without building artificial security obstacles which then had to be overcome.
sentences.zh: 我们还有很多其他领域可以发挥聪明才智，而无需建立必须克服的人为安全障碍。

blocks.html_en: Yet when I say I am a hacker, people often think I am making a naughty admission, presenting myself specifically as a security breaker. How did this confusion develop?

sentences.en: Yet when I say I am a hacker, people often think I am making a naughty admission, presenting myself specifically as a security breaker.
sentences.zh: 然而，当我说我是一名黑客时，人们常常认为我在顽皮地承认自己，专门将自己表现为安全破坏者。

sentences.en: How did this confusion develop?
sentences.zh: 这种混乱是如何发展的？

blocks.html_en: Around 1980, when the news media took notice of hackers, they fixated on one narrow aspect of real hacking: the security breaking which some hackers occasionally did. They ignored all the rest of hacking, and took the term to mean breaking security, no more and no less. The media have since spread that definition, disregarding our attempts to correct them. As a result, most people have a mistaken idea of what we hackers actually do and what we think.

sentences.en: Around 1980, when the news media took notice of hackers, they fixated on one narrow aspect of real hacking: the security breaking which some hackers occasionally did.
sentences.zh: 1980 年左右，当新闻媒体注意到黑客时，他们只关注真正黑客攻击的一个狭隘方面：一些黑客偶尔会破坏安全。

sentences.en: They ignored all the rest of hacking, and took the term to mean breaking security, no more and no less.
sentences.zh: 他们忽略了所有其他的黑客攻击，并认为这个术语意味着破坏安全，不多也不少。

sentences.en: The media have since spread that definition, disregarding our attempts to correct them.
sentences.zh: 此后，媒体传播了这个定义，无视我们纠正它们的努力。

sentences.en: As a result, most people have a mistaken idea of what we hackers actually do and what we think.
sentences.zh: 结果，大多数人对我们黑客的实际行为和想法产生了错误的认识。

blocks.html_en: You can help correct the misunderstanding simply by making a distinction between security breaking and hacking—by using the term "cracking" for security breaking. The people who do it are "crackers" (***). Some of them may also be hackers, just as some of them may be chess players or golfers; most of them are not.

sentences.en: You can help correct the misunderstanding simply by making a distinction between security breaking and hacking—by using the term "cracking" for security breaking.
sentences.zh: 您可以通过简单地区分安全破坏和黑客攻击（使用术语“破解”来表示安全破坏）来帮助纠正误解。

sentences.en: The people who do it are "crackers" (***).
sentences.zh: 这样做的人都是“cracker”（***）。

sentences.en: Some of them may also be hackers, just as some of them may be chess players or golfers; most of them are not.
sentences.zh: 他们中的一些人也可能是黑客，就像他们中的一些人可能是国际象棋运动员或高尔夫球手一样；大多数人都不是。

blocks.html_en: Happy hacking.

sentences.en: Happy hacking.
sentences.zh: 快乐黑客。

blocks.html_en: ** Going on the great dome is "forbidden", so in a sense it constitutes "breaking security". Nonetheless, the MIT Museum proudly presents photos of some of the best dome hacks, as well as some of the objects that hackers placed on the dome in their hacks. The MIT administration thus implicitly recognizes that "breaking security" is not inherently evil and need not be invariably condemned. Whether security breaking is wrong depends on what the security breaker proceeds to do with the "forbidden" access thus obtained. Hurting people is bad, amusing the community is good.

sentences.en: The MIT administration thus implicitly recognizes that "breaking security" is not inherently evil and need not be invariably condemned.
sentences.zh: 因此，麻省理工学院政府含蓄地认识到“破坏安全”本质上并不是邪恶的，因此不必总是受到谴责。

sentences.en: Whether security breaking is wrong depends on what the security breaker proceeds to do with the "forbidden" access thus obtained.
sentences.zh: 安全破坏是否错误取决于安全破坏者如何处理由此获得的“禁止”访问。

• In challenge-level square dance, the caller invents combinations of meta-calls, and the dancers have to figure out very quickly what those calls mean in terms of physical motion. It is not easy, and the set gets messed up from time to time. One caller at MIT around 1980 had a habit of saying "damn it" when that happened.

    The dancers were more or less the same group at each session, and being at MIT, they decided to hack the caller: they defined "damn it" as a call, but didn't tell him. They defined the call to mean, "Change places with your corner" — chosen because it would never help clean up the mess. Subsequently, each time he said "damn it," he got a puzzling surprise.

sentences.en: They defined the call to mean, "Change places with your corner" — chosen because it would never help clean up the mess.

• You can make Nike's running-map server display whatever drawing you like by running on properly chosen streets.

  • "Rooftoppers" scale tall buildings just for the hack of it. I don't share, and can't understand, their desire for risk, but that doesn't alter the fact that this is hacking.

  • Acción Ortográfica Quito corrects punctuation and grammar in graffiti.

  • A German student filed a freedom of information request to get the questions for an exam he will have to take.

  • A hacker arranged to play music by printing on a dot-matrix printer. Here's one with a line printer. Note that the line printer is not being told to advance the paper.

  • Japanese artist Megumi Igarashi is on trial for distributing 3d-printed models of her genitals.

    She also built a kayak using that shape. Paddling such a kayak would enable certain fetishists to feel they are really inside her.

  • Airline "hobbyists" hack the rules of frequent flier miles to get lots of air travel without ever needing to pay.

    I appreciate the cleverness of these hacks, but repeating the hack every day seems pointless as well as extremely wasteful — like an addiction. Once should be enough.

  • Russian pranksters fooled Elton John by phoning him and pretending to be President Putin.

  • Shoppers at Zara stores found clothes with labels saying, "I Made This... But Didn't Get Paid".
  • Lenny the robo-answerer can waste the time of robo-callers. As of January 2018 you can phone Lenny at +1 347-514-7296.

2000年6月，在访问韩国时，我做了一次有趣的黑客活动，清楚地说明了“黑客”一词的原始和真正含义。

我和一些 GNU 粉丝一起去吃午饭，正坐下来吃一些炒年糕 (*)，这时一位女服务员在我面前放下了六根筷子。 我突然想到，也许这些是为三个人准备的，但更有趣的是想象我应该使用所有六个人。 我不知道有什么方法可以做到这一点，所以我意识到如果我能想出一种方法，那就是一种破解。 我开始思考。 几秒钟后我有了一个想法。

首先我用左手把三根筷子放到右手里。 这并不难，尽管我必须弄清楚将它们放在哪里以便我可以单独控制它们。 然后我用右手把另外三根筷子放到了左手上。 这很困难，因为我必须防止右手已有的三根筷子掉下来。 经过几次尝试，我完成了。

然后我必须弄清楚如何使用这六根筷子。 那更难了。 我的左手控制得不太好，但我右手却成功地操纵了这三个动作。 经过几分钟的练习和调整，我成功地用三根棍子从三个不同的方向汇聚在一块食物上，夹起一块食物，放进嘴里。

这并不容易——出于实用目的，使用两根筷子是完全优越的。 但正是因为一只手使用三个是困难的并且通常从未想到过，所以它具有“黑客价值”，正如我的午餐同伴立即意识到的那样。 开玩笑地做一些困难的事情，无论有用与否，那就是黑客行为。

后来我向波士顿的一位朋友讲述了韩国的故事，他把四根筷子放在一只手上，并把它们分成两对——同时夹起两块不同的食物，每双一根。 他已经超越了我的黑客。 他的行为也是黑客行为吗？ 我想是的。 那么他是一名黑客吗？ 这取决于他有多喜欢黑客。

黑客社区在 20 世纪 60 年代和 1970 年代在麻省理工学院和其他一些大学发展起来。 黑客活动涉及范围广泛，从编写软件到恶作剧，再到探索麻省理工学院校园的屋顶和隧道。 其他远离麻省理工学院、远离计算机进行的活动也符合黑客对黑客行为的理解：例如，我认为约翰·凯奇 (John Cage) 创作的备受争议的 20 世纪 50 年代“音乐作品”，4'33" (****)，与其说是音乐作品，不如说是黑客行为。 纪尧姆·德·马肖 (Guillaume de Machaut) 在 1300 年代创作的回文三部分作品“Ma Fin Est Mon Commencement”也是一个很好的技巧，甚至更好，因为它作为音乐听起来也很不错。 帕克很欣赏黑客的价值。

很难为黑客这样多种多样的活动写出一个简单的定义，但我认为这些活动的共同点是好玩、聪明和探索。 因此，黑客意味着本着俏皮聪明的精神探索可能性的极限。 表现出俏皮聪明的活动具有“黑客价值”。

黑客的概念排除了智慧和艺术本身。 那些开始将他们的活动称为“黑客”的人们熟悉智慧和艺术，以及这些领域的各个领域的名称；他们还做了一些其他的事情，一些不同的事情，为此他们想出了“黑客”这个名字。 因此，创作一个有趣的笑话或一首优美的音乐很可能需要俏皮的聪明才智，但一个笑话本身和一首音乐本身并不是黑客，无论它们多么有趣或美丽。 然而，如果这首曲子是回文，我们可以说它是黑客，也是音乐；如果这首曲子是空洞的，我们可以说它是对音乐的黑客攻击。

黑客通常不太尊重管理员喜欢强加的愚蠢规则，因此他们寻找解决方法。 例如，当麻省理工学院的计算机开始具有“安全性”（即对用户可以做什么的限制）时，一些黑客找到了绕过安全性的巧妙方法，部分是为了他们可以自由地使用计算机，部分只是为了聪明（黑客攻击不一定有用）。 然而，只有一些黑客做到了这一点——许多黑客都忙于其他类型的聪明才智，例如在麻省理工学院的大圆顶上放置一些有趣的物体（**），找到一种方法在已知最短的程序需要 6 条指令时只用 5 条指令进行某种计算，编写一个程序来打印罗马数字的数字，或者编写一个程序来理解英语问题。 （黑客攻击不一定没有实际用途。）

与此同时，麻省理工学院的另一组黑客找到了解决计算机安全问题的不同解决方案：他们设计了没有安全“功能”的不兼容分时系统。 在黑客的天堂、人工智能实验室的辉煌岁月里，没有安全漏洞，因为没有安全可破解。 正是在那里，在那种环境下，我学会了成为一名黑客，尽管我之前已经表现出了这种倾向。 我们还有很多其他领域可以发挥聪明才智，而无需建立必须克服的人为安全障碍。

然而，当我说我是一名黑客时，人们常常认为我在顽皮地承认自己，专门将自己表现为安全破坏者。 这种混乱是如何发展的？

1980 年左右，当新闻媒体注意到黑客时，他们只关注真正黑客攻击的一个狭隘方面：一些黑客偶尔会破坏安全。 他们忽略了所有其他的黑客攻击，并认为这个术语意味着破坏安全，不多也不少。 此后，媒体传播了这个定义，无视我们纠正它们的努力。 结果，大多数人对我们黑客的实际行为和想法产生了错误的认识。

您可以通过简单地区分安全破坏和黑客攻击（使用术语“破解”来表示安全破坏）来帮助纠正误解。 这样做的人都是“cracker”（***）。 他们中的一些人也可能是黑客，就像他们中的一些人可能是国际象棋运动员或高尔夫球手一样；大多数人都不是。

快乐黑客。

** 登上大圆顶是“禁止的”，因此从某种意义上来说，这构成了“破坏安全”。 尽管如此，麻省理工学院博物馆仍然自豪地展示了一些最好的圆顶黑客的照片，以及黑客在黑客攻击中放置在圆顶上的一些物体。 因此，麻省理工学院政府含蓄地认识到“破坏安全”本质上并不是邪恶的，因此不必总是受到谴责。 安全破坏是否错误取决于安全破坏者如何处理由此获得的“禁止”访问。 伤害别人是坏事，逗乐社会则是好事。
